title: DBMSolver: A Training-free Diffusion Bridge Samplerfor High-Quality Image-to-Image Translation

paper.title: DBMSolver: A Training-free Diffusion Bridge Sampler for High-Quality Image-to-Image Translation
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion-based image-to-image (I2I) translation excels in high-fidelity generation but suffers from slow sampling in state-of-the-art Diffusion Bridge Models (DBMs), often requiring dozens of function evaluations (NFEs). We introduce DBMSolver , a training-free sampler that exploits the semi-linear structure of DBM’s underlying SDE and ODE via exponential integrators, yielding highly-efficient 1 st 1^{\text{st}} - and 2 nd 2^{\text{nd}} -order solutions. This reduces NFEs by up to 5 × 5\times while boosting quality (e.g., FID drops 53 % 53\% on DIODE at 20 NFEs vs. 2 nd 2^{\text{nd}} -order baseline). Experiments on inpainting, stylization, and semantics-to-image tasks across resolutions up to 256 × \times 256 show DBMSolver sets new SOTA efficiency-quality tradeoffs, enabling real-world applicability. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/snumprlab/dbmsolver .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Image-to-Image (I2I) Translation is a generative modeling paradigm that learns to map an input image to a target output. It encompasses tasks like image restoration, grayscale colorization, and inpainting of occluded or corrupted regions, as well as style transfer and semantic reinterpretation via cross-domain synthesis [ 36 , 14 , 7 ] . Recent diffusion-based works, as alternatives to traditional generative approaches such as GANs [ 45 , 16 ] , have brought significant advances in the synthesis of high-fidelity images [ 29 , 22 , 17 ] . Among them, [ 44 ] proposed Diffusion Bridge Models (DBMs), capable of performing I2I Translation by establishing a diffusion bridge that facilitates the translation from one arbitrary image distribution to another. While DBMs offer a theoretically elegant diffusion framework for I2I Translation, generating high-quality images using such diffusion-based models remains computationally expensive, as it requires numerous costly function evaluations (NFEs)–which we aim to tackle in this work without requiring any additional training overhead . DBMSolver: A Training-free Diffusion Bridge Sampler for High-Quality Image-to-Image Translation presents the fact that while Hybrid Heun [ 44 ] and DBIM [ 42 ] require numerous NFEs for coherent or high-quality outputs on DIODE [ 37 ] , our method (DBMSolver) achieves superior fidelity in just 6 NFEs, preserving intricate details like tree branches without artifacts. Unlike DBIM’s linear multistep methods [ 42 ] or audio-specific EI in Bridge-TTS [ 2 ] , DBMSolver derives closed-form solutions for VP/VE bridges, avoiding crude approximations and enabling FID gains even at low NFEs.

sections.heading: 1.1 DBMSolver Overview
sections.text: We introduce DBMSolver : a training-free, highly efficient solver specifically designed to accelerate the DBM-based sampling process. Previous research on improving the sampling speeds explored either model distillation [ 9 , 40 , 8 ] , fine-tuning [ 6 , 9 ] , or re-training of an entire neural network [ 43 ] . In contrast, DBMSolver is a drop-in replacement for existing DBM sampling methods, avoiding the need for any architectural changes or extra training, thus enabling broad compatibility and immediate benefits. We devise DBMSolver by rigorously analyzing the underlying Stochastic and Ordinary Differential Equations (SDE and ODE) governing DBMs’ reverse-time diffusion process (Equations 2 and 5 ). Specifically, in Section 3.2 , we identify the inherent semi-linear structure of the SDE and leverage the Exponential Integrators (EI) [ 12 ] method to derive an efficient 1 st 1^{\text{st}} -order solution. Next, in Section 3.3 , we analyze the ODE to show that it has a semi-linear structure as well, allowing us to formulate an exact solution that we efficiently approximate with a 2 nd 2^{\text{nd}} -order solution. By combining the two ODE/SDE solutions, we devise a sampling procedure that drastically reduces the required NFEs while enhancing the image quality, as showcased in Section 3.4 . The key contributions of this work are as follows: • A novel, training-free bridge sampler : DBMSolver accelerates DBM sampling by 20x (e.g., 6 NFEs vs. 119 for Hybrid Heun) on conditional/unconditional I2I tasks, with zero retraining–unlike distillation [ 9 ] or fine-tuning [ 8 ] approaches. • Theoretically grounded : We provide analytical solutions for the Bridge SDE and ODE governing DBMs, grounded in diffusion bridge theory. • State-of-the-art performances on various I2I tasks : Through extensive experimentation on various I2I tasks and image resolutions, we show that DBMSolver consistently achieves state-of-the-art results, outperforming prior arts [ 42 , 20 , 39 ] in terms of generation quality and computational efficiency.

sections.heading: Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DPMs).
sections.text: Owing to their ability to generate high-quality outputs, DPMs have become ubiquitous for various noise-to-image generation tasks [ 28 , 15 ] . DPMs learn to traverse from a Gaussian distribution p prior ​ ( 𝐱 ) p_{\text{prior}}(\mathbf{x}) to an unknown data distribution p 0 ​ ( 𝐱 ) := p data ​ ( 𝐱 ) p_{0}(\mathbf{x}):=p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x}) through a gradual denoising process [ 11 , 33 , 4 ] . In other words, starting from a prior distribution p T ​ ( 𝐱 ) := p prior ​ ( 𝐱 ) ≈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , σ T 2 ​ I ) p_{T}(\mathbf{x}):=p_{\text{prior}}(\mathbf{x})\approx\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma_{T}^{2}\,\textbf{I}) with σ T > 0 \sigma_{T}>0 , DPMs iteratively denoise 𝒙 T ∼ p T ​ ( 𝐱 ) \boldsymbol{x}_{T}\sim p_{T}(\mathbf{x}) ( i.e. , white noise) to recover the desired output 𝒙 0 ∼ p 0 ​ ( 𝐱 ) \boldsymbol{x}_{0}\sim p_{0}(\mathbf{x}) . This reverse diffusion process is shown to follow the Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) [ 1 , 33 ] : d ​ 𝒙 t = [ f ⁡ ( 𝒙 t , t ) − 1 2 ​ g ​ ( t ) 2 ​ ∇ 𝒙 t ​ log ⁡ p t ​ ( 𝒙 ) ] ​ d ​ t , \text{d}{\boldsymbol{x}_{t}}=\left[\,f({\boldsymbol{x}_{t},t})-\frac{1}{2}g({t})^{2}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}_{t}}\log{p_{t}}({\boldsymbol{x}})\right]\text{d}{t}, (1) where p t ​ ( 𝐱 ) p_{t}(\mathbf{x}) is the marginal distribution of 𝒙 t \boldsymbol{x}_{t} at t t , and ∇ 𝒙 t ​ log ​ p t ​ ( 𝐱 ) \nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}_{t}}\log{p_{t}}({\mathbf{x}}) is its score function learned by a neural network [ 13 ] , and f ⁡ ( 𝒙 t , t ) \,f({\boldsymbol{x}_{t},t}) and g ⁡ ( t ) g({t}) are the drift and diffusion coefficients, respectively (see Supplementary). sections.heading: Diffusion Bridge Models (DBMs).
2.2 Fast Samplers for DMs and DBMs
sections.text: For DPM-based N2I Generation, works such as [ 24 , 23 , 41 ] proposed fast samplers that generate high-quality images in ≤ 20 \leq 20 NFEs. These methods follow the assumption that the prior is a pure Gaussian distribution. However, since this assumption becomes invalid for I2I Translation (as prior p T ​ ( 𝐱 ) p_{T}(\mathbf{x}) can be arbitrary), their theoretical foundation is unsuitable for I2I tasks, calling for samplers that support arbitrary priors. Table 1 contrasts samplers, highlighting why N2I methods (e.g., DDIM [ 31 ] ) fail on DBMs: their Gaussian prior assumption breaks when p T ​ ( 𝐱 ) p_{T}(\mathbf{x}) is not Gaussian, leading to an invalid bridge (see Supp. for examples). To generate high-quality images with DBMs, [ 44 ] proposed the Hybrid Heun (HH) Sampler, which alternatively solves the Bridge SDE ( Equation 2 ) via 1 st 1^{\text{st}} -order Euler-Maruyama and the Bridge PF ODE ( Equation 5 ) via 2 nd 2^{\text{nd}} -order Heun. Next, inspired by [ 31 ] , [ 42 ] proposed a non-Markovian 1 st 1^{\text{st}} -order sampler called DBIM (“DBIM-1”). “DBIM-2” and “DBIM-3” have also been proposed, derived via Linear Multistep methods analogous to DPMSolver++(2M) [ 23 ] , serving as 2 nd 2^{\text{nd}} - and 3 rd 3^{\text{rd}} -order samplers, respectively. A recent finding, ODES3 [ 39 ] , implements a straightforward algorithm with 1 st 1^{\text{st}} -order Euler-Maruyama initial step with the Bridge SDE and subsequent 2 nd 2^{\text{nd}} -order Heun steps with the Bridge ODE. In contrast, we analyze and rigorously derive exact solutions for the Bridge SDE and ODE to propose a highly-efficient 2 nd 2^{\text{nd}} -order sampler that surpasses prior works in image quality and efficiency. DBMSolver is capable of handling arbitrary priors while achieving better results compared to previous HH, DBIM-2/3, and ODES3 samplers.

sections.heading: 3 DBMSolver: A Fast DBM Sampler
sections.text: DBMs’ diffusion bridge introduces non-Gaussian drifts that N2I solvers do not take into account. We uncover their overlooked semi-linear form–linear in 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} with non-linear scores–and provide exact linear-term solutions that prior works missed. The fundamental difference between DPMs and DBMs is that 𝒙 T \boldsymbol{x}_{T} is pure noise for DPMs, but it can be an arbitrary image for DBMs. Consequently, DBMs involve a reverse diffusion process conditioned on 𝒙 T \boldsymbol{x}_{T} , which is crucial for I2I Translation. As discussed in Section 2.2 , this crucial distinction invalidates the direct application of state-of-the-art fast N2I solvers [ 23 ] for sampling DBMs. We explore a different approach to developing fast samplers specifically for DBMs by thoroughly analyzing their underlying reverse diffusion SDE and ODE (Eqs. 2 & 5 ), and deriving analytic solutions that eliminate approximation errors associated with the linear terms using Exponential Integrators (EI) [ 12 ] . With these solutions, we develop a higher-order sampling procedure that generates high-quality images significantly faster, tailored for DBMs. Let D 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒙 s , s , 𝒙 T , T ) \textbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{s},s,\boldsymbol{x}_{T},T) denote an 𝒙 0 \boldsymbol{x}_{0} -predicting DBM such that D 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒙 s , s , 𝒙 T , T ) ≈ 𝒙 0 \textbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{s},s,\boldsymbol{x}_{T},T)\approx\boldsymbol{x}_{0} for s ∈ [ 0 , T ] s\in[0,T] . For brevity, we adopt D 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒙 s ) := D 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒙 s , s , 𝒙 T , T ) \textbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{s}):=\textbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{s},s,\boldsymbol{x}_{T},T) .

sections.heading: 3.3 Deriving the Solution to the Bridge PF ODE
sections.text: Having set grounds with Proposition 1 , we next focus on the Bridge PF ODE ( Equation 5 ). Similar to the Bridge SDE analysis above, we show that the Bridge ODE also exhibits semi-linearity in its structure, which has been largely overlooked in prior work. We take advantage of this property and derive a closed-form exact solution through the EI method. We then utilize the change-of-variables method to reformulate the solution as an exponentially-weighted integral. Finally, we analytically minimize discretization errors by approximating via the Taylor-expansion of this integral, yielding a fast and efficient sampling procedure, as presented in Proposition 2 with proof in Supplementary. sections.heading: Initial Step.
sections.text: We observe that our solution of the Bridge PF ODE in Equation 9 is only valid for time t < T t<T , which implies that it cannot be employed for an initial step from s = T s=T to time t < T t<T . This is because, as s → T s\rightarrow T , ρ ⁡ ( λ s , λ T ) → ρ ⁡ ( λ T , λ T ) = 0 \rho(\lambda_{s},\lambda_{T})\rightarrow\rho(\lambda_{T},\lambda_{T})=0 which would cause the coefficient of 𝒙 s \boldsymbol{x}_{s} to diverge to infinity. We instead employ the 1 st 1^{\text{st}} -order Bridge SDE solution ( Equation 8 ) exclusively for this initial step from s = T s=T to t = T − ϵ t=T-\epsilon ( ϵ ≈ \epsilon\approx 1e-4), and the regular Bridge PF ODE solution ( Equation 9 ) for the subsequent steps (where t < s ≤ T − ϵ t<s\leq T-\epsilon ), as described next.

sections.heading: Subsequent Steps.
sections.text: Higher-order formulations of Equation 10 can lead to a sampling procedure capable of generating high-quality images more efficiently, as demonstrated in previous work [ 24 , 23 , 41 ] . This improvement stems from the fact that higher-order Taylor-approximations have smaller error bounds, yielding more accurate approximations. Following this idea, we set k = 2 k=2 , resulting in a 2 nd 2^{\text{nd}} -order Bridge ODE solution for Equation 9 . We adopt this 2 nd 2^{\text{nd}} -order formulation for DBMSolver (complete derivation in Supplementary) and provide the rationale below.

sections.heading: Summarizing DBMSolver’s Algorithm.
sections.text: Given time steps T = t N > t N − 1 > ⋯ > t 1 > t 0 = 0 T=t_{N}>t_{N-1}>\dots>t_{1}>t_{0}=0 , we first compute 𝒙 ~ t N − 1 \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}_{t_{N-1}} from prior image 𝒙 t N ∼ p T ​ ( 𝒙 ) \boldsymbol{x}_{t_{N}}\sim p_{T}(\boldsymbol{x}) using Equation 8 . For the next N − 2 N-2 steps, we iteratively apply Equation 9 with k = 2 k=2 , yielding better approximations for each intermediate noisy sample until 𝒙 ~ t 1 \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}_{t_{1}} . To obtain the final 𝒙 ~ 0 \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}_{0} prediction, we solve the Bridge PF ODE from t 1 t_{1} to t 0 t_{0} using the widely used Euler method, resulting in a high-fidelity output. We summarize it in Algorithm 1 and validate it empirically in the next section.

sections.heading: Rationale for DBMSolver Order Selection.
sections.text: As mentioned above, our method involves two distinct integration phases. For the initial Bridge SDE step , we employ the 1 st 1^{\text{st}} -order solution Proposition 1 . Our rationale is that this step is taken over a very small interval d ​ t = ϵ \text{d}t=\epsilon , rendering the marginal accuracy gains from a higher-order approximation unnecessary. Nonetheless, for completeness, we present derivations for higher-order Bridge SDE solutions in the Supplementary. For the subsequent Bridge ODE steps , we note that k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 involves a non-elementary antiderivative , meaning its solution cannot be expressed in closed form using elementary functions (e.g., polynomials, exponentials, or logarithms). While such equations can be addressed using numerical techniques like linear multistep methods, an approach adopted by DBIM [ 42 ] for their higher-order (DBIM-2 and DBIM-3) samplers, we instead avoid this associated complexity and larger error bounds. As the experiments in Section 4.1 will show, our 2nd-order DBMSolver significantly outperforms [ 42 ] ’s 1st-order DBIM-1 and the numerically approximated higher-order DBIM-2 and DBIM-3. Therefore, we restrict DBMSolver to the k = 2 k=2 ( 2 nd 2^{\text{nd}} -order) solution, which remains analytically tractable. Ablations in Supplementary confirm k = 2 k=2 generates better FID scores than k = 1 k=1 (DBIM-1’s analog). sections.heading: 4 Experiments and Results
sections.text: We conducted extensive experiments to evaluate DBMSolver against established baselines on various I2I Translation tasks, including conditional image inpainting and semantics-to-image generation, to demonstrate its versatility across diverse tasks. Specifically, we evaluate the following datasets: Sketch-to-Image on Edges2Handbags (E2H) [ 14 ] , Surface normals-to-Image on DIODE-Outdoor [ 37 ] , Face-to-Comic stylization on Face2Comics (F2C), Conditional Image Inpainting with central masks on ImageNet [ 3 ] , and Semantic Label-to-Face generation on CelebAMask-HQ [ 18 ] . We benchmark against DDBM (Hybrid Heun) [ 44 ] , DBIM variants (1st/2nd/3rd-order) [ 42 ] . Note that, DBIM-2/3 use their multistep numerics for higher order. Additional baselines of DDIB [ 34 ] , SDEdit [ 25 ] , and I 2 {}^{\text{2}} SB [ 22 ] are evaluated following the DDBM and DBIM protocols. We mainly assess sampling quality using FID [ 10 ] , MSE, IS, and LPIPS, and computational efficiency via the number of forward evaluations NFEs [ 31 , 24 ] , following prior works [ 44 , 42 ] . For CelebAMask-HQ, we additionally report the classification accuracy (CA), following [ 20 ] . We use the publicly available DBM checkpoints from [ 44 ] for E2H and DIODE, highlighting DBMSolver’s training-free integration. For ImageNet inpainting, we adopt the DBM checkpoint from [ 42 ] , which was finetuned via I 2 {}^{\text{2}} SB [ 22 ] from a pre-trained N2I Diffusion Model. For datasets lacking checkpoints (e.g., Face2Comics, CelebAMask-HQ), we train DBMs from scratch using the ADM U-Net [ 4 ] , following standard diffusion architectures. sections.text: Table 2 reports FID scores and NFEs across methods. DBMSolver achieves state-of-the-art results with significantly fewer evaluations. At just 6 NFEs, it achieves FID scores of 0.97 (E2H) and 3.38 (DIODE), outperforming Hybrid Heun and DBIM-1/2/3. Its high efficiency at low NFEs enables rapid sampling, making it well-suited for real-time DBM applications by supporting faster generation and higher throughput. It exhibits strong scalability with increasing NFEs, yielding further improvements in FID. The trends in Figure 2 -a,b show that as NFE increases, DBMSolver quickly achieves high fidelity and remains stable. Figure 3 supports this, indicating that even at low NFEs (e.g., 6), DBMSolver and DBIM generate visually rich, coherent outputs, outperforming others in detail and realism. DPMSolver++2M preserves structure but lacks vibrant colors and texture, especially at lower NFEs. While DBIM yields appealing outputs, it lacks fine detail compared to our method– a gap reflected in FID and trend metrics. Please refer to the intricate structural details observable in the tree branches and twigs within the DIODE images, as well as the fine-grained textures and contours present in the handbag depictions. At as low as 6 NFEs, DBMSolver achieves an FID of 34.76 (in Figure 5 ) outperforming DBIM-1’s 44.92 as well as GAN-based models and other diffusion approaches, while using significantly fewer NFEs. Visually, DBMSolver preserves fine structural details such as eye contours, hairlines, and mask edges, which are often blurred or distorted in DBIM outputs. sections.heading: Relation to Schrödinger Bridges.
sections.text: We distinguish our work from methods addressing the Schrödinger Bridge (SB) problem, such as [ 2 ] . SB methods solve a specific, entropy-regularized optimal transport problem; [ 2 ] , for example, assumes a “tractable” SB formulation that results in a specific set of bridge SDEs/ODEs. Our approach is distinct. DBMSolver is a general-purpose solver derived specifically for the generalized VP/VE-Bridge framework of [ 44 ] , which unifies VP, VE, and Brownian bridge constructions. Because DBMs’ [ 44 ] underlying framework is different from SB, our resulting Bridge SDEs/ODE solutions (Propositions 1 and 2 ) are also fundamentally different. Therefore, while [ 2 ] derives solutions for their specific SB equations, DBMSolver is a novel solver tailored to the SDEs/ODEs of the generalized VP/VE-Bridge [ 44 ] framework. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduce DBMSolver, a principled, training-free sampler that significantly enhances the efficiency and quality of diffusion bridge-based I2I translation. By leveraging the semi-linear structure of the Bridge SDE and PF ODE, DBMSolver accelerates sampling without compromising fidelity. Experiments on diverse datasets such as Edges2Handbags, DIODE-Outdoor, Face2Comics, CelebAMask-HQ, and ImageNet Inpainting show that DBMSolver sets a new benchmark for efficient diffusion bridge models and marking a step toward the practical deployment of powerful solvers for I2I Translation.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work.
sections.text: A limitation is that DBMSolver performed similarly to previous solvers on more realistic tasks like ImageNet Inpainting, which we hypothesize is due to the non-linear 𝑫 𝜽 \boldsymbol{D_{\theta}} term being the main cause of approximation errors. Exploring DBMs for text-conditioned I2I translation, adaptive stepsize for DBM sampling, or integration with flow-matching [ 21 ] , are also promising avenues for research.
